title: Time value of money and choosing projects
subtitle: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year. Put every cash flow on one date and the choice becomes arithmetic.

sections.title: Why money has a time value
sections.body:
Would you rather have Rs 1,000 today or Rs 1,000 a year from now? Today, of course, and not just out of impatience: money today can be invested to earn a return, so Rs 1,000 today can become more later. That is the time value of money, and the whole chapter is built on it.

Simple interest is earned only on the principal; compound interest earns interest on interest: F = P(1 + i)ⁿ. Watch it snowball. With P = 1,000, i = 10 % and n = 5, F = 1000(1.1)⁵ = 1610.51. So at 10 % for 5 years, Rs 1,000 grows to Rs 1,611. Turn it round, and Rs 1,000 in 5 years is worth only Rs 621 today. Compared with simple interest, compound interest gives you more, and the gap widens every year.

questions.prompt: Compared with simple interest, compound interest gives…

problems.prompt: How much will Rs 5,000 be worth in 8 years at 6 % compound interest?

keynotes: Money can be invested to earn a return, so a rupee today is worth more than a rupee later.
Simple interest is earned only on the principal; compound interest earns interest on interest: F = P(1 + i)ⁿ.
At 10 % for 5 years Rs 1,000 grows to Rs 1,611; equivalently Rs 1,000 in 5 years is worth only Rs 621 today.

sections.title: Equivalence and the cash-flow diagram
sections.body:
How do you compare Rs 1,000 now with Rs 350 a year for four years? You need a common yardstick. Two cash flows are equivalent if they have the same worth at the same date and interest rate, and a cash-flow diagram is the picture that lets you see it. Time runs along a horizontal axis, inflows are up arrows and outflows are down arrows. The initial investment is therefore a down arrow at time zero.

Below, we invest 1,000 now and receive 350 at the end of each of 4 years, at MARR = 8 %. Look at the card: it shows present worth, future worth, IRR and more. Everything in this chapter is about turning arrows like these into a single comparable number.

sections.title: The six interest factors
sections.body:
Six little factors do all the converting between a present sum P, a future sum F and a uniform yearly payment A. Think of them as a currency-exchange table between dates. You do not need to memorise it; you need to know where to look.

To findGivenFactor
FP(1 + i)ⁿ
PF(1 + i)⁻ⁿ
PA[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] / [i(1 + i)ⁿ]
APi(1 + i)ⁿ / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]
FA[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] / i
AFi / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]

Annuity A is a uniform end-of-period payment. Let’s use it. The P/A factor at 8 %, n = 4 is (1.08⁴ − 1)/(0.08 · 1.08⁴) = 3.3121. Multiply by the annuity amount 350 and P = 350 × 3.3121 = 1159.24. So the present worth of 350 a year for 4 years at 8 % is 1159.24. Going the other way, repaying a Rs 1,000 loan over 4 years costs 301.92 a year. To spread a loan P over n years, which factor do you want? The one that takes P to A.

sections.title: Nominal and effective rates
sections.body:
A bank advertises 12 % “compounded monthly”. Is that really 12 %? Not quite. A nominal 12 % compounded monthly is 1 % per month, and compounding within the year makes the effective annual rate (1 + r/m)ᵐ − 1 = 12.68 %, more than 12 %. Interest on interest, again, but now every month.

Try another: a nominal 18 % compounded quarterly is 4.5 % per quarter, and the effective annual rate is (1.045)⁴ − 1 = 19.25 %. The rule to carry away: always match the interest period to the payment period. Monthly payments need a monthly rate.

questions.prompt: Nominal 12 % compounded monthly has an effective rate that is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Interest on interest inside the year.

keynotes: A nominal 12 % compounded monthly is 1 % per month, with effective annual rate (1 + r/m)ᵐ − 1 = 12.68 %.
A nominal 18 % compounded quarterly is 4.5 % per quarter, an effective 19.25 %.
Always match the interest period to the payment period.

sections.title: Present worth and MARR
sections.body:
Before you build anything, ask: is this project worth doing at all? Every firm sets a bar called the minimum attractive rate of return (MARR), the least return it will accept. Then net present worth, NPW = Σ Cₜ/(1 + MARR)ᵗ, turns the whole project into one number. If NPW > 0 the project earns more than MARR, so accept.

Test it on project A at 8 %: NPW = −1000 + 350·(P/A) = 159.24. Project B (invest 1,500, receive 500 a year) gives 156.06. Both are worth doing on their own; but only one can be built. Compare B’s present worth with A’s in the figure. If NPW > 0 at the MARR, what does it mean for the project? That it beats your bar.

choices.text: The project earns more than the MARR: accept.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — project B
figures.note: Compare its present worth with project A.

keynotes: MARR is the minimum attractive rate of return, the least return the firm will accept.

sections.title: Internal rate of return
sections.body:
NPW answers “how much better than the bar?”. The IRR asks the opposite question: what return does this project earn on its own? It is the rate that makes NPW = 0, and you accept if IRR > MARR.

For project A the IRR is ≈ 14.96 %; for project B, 12.59 %. Both beat 8 %. How is it found? By trial: try i = 15 %, then NPW = −1000 + 350 × 2.855 = −0.76. That is almost zero, so the IRR is just under 15 %. There is no closed form for n > 4, so use the card’s solver. Make sure you can say in words what the IRR is: the discount rate at which NPW is zero.

worked.why: That is almost zero, so the IRR is just under 15 %.

questions.prompt: The IRR is the discount rate at which…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Inflows exactly repay outflows with interest.

keynotes: The IRR is the rate that makes NPW = 0; accept if IRR > MARR.
Project A has IRR ≈ 14.96 % and project B 12.59 %, both beating 8 %.
It is found by trial or a solver; there is no closed form for n > 4.

sections.title: Comparing alternatives: incremental analysis
sections.body:
Here is a trap that catches even experienced people. Only one of A and B can be built, so which wins? You might say the one with the larger IRR, but the larger IRR does not always win, and a bigger investment is justified only if its extra money earns enough. So we study the increment B − A.

The extra investment is 500, for an extra return of 150 a year over four years, and the incremental IRR is ≈ 7.71 %. That is below the MARR of 8 %, so the extra 500 is not worth spending: choose A. (This agrees with NPW(A) = 159.24 > NPW(B) = 156.06, even though B has the larger returns.) A rule of thumb for you: compare equal-life options by NPW, and unequal lives by annual worth, which repeats each as if replaced. If the incremental IRR falls below MARR, drop the bigger one.

sections.title: Benefit–cost ratio and payback
sections.body:
Governments building a bridge, as you can imagine, cannot ask “what is the IRR?”, so public projects use a simpler idea: benefits against costs. B/C = PW(benefits)/PW(costs); accept if > 1. For project A, PW(benefits) = 350 × 3.3121 = 1159.2 and PW(costs) = 1000, so B/C = 1159.2/1000 = 1.16, greater than 1: accept at 8 %.

Then there is payback, the time to recover the investment: simple payback for A = 1000/350 = 2.86 years. It is easy to understand and easy to misuse, because it ignores the time value and any cash flows after payback. So use it only as a rough liquidity check. What is its weakness in a sentence? It ignores everything that happens after the money is back.

questions.prompt: A weakness of simple payback is that it…

choices.text: Ignores the time value of money and later cash flows.

keynotes: Public projects use B/C = PW(benefits)/PW(costs) and accept if it is greater than 1.
For project A, B/C = 1159.2/1000 = 1.16, so accept at 8 %.
